lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7 you met England's Bill of Rights. In which year was it passed? (1689.) Today: the Enlightenment's ideas about rights, and the revolutions in America, France and Haiti that claimed them.

The Enlightenment was a movement of the 1700s. Its writers argued that reason and evidence, not only tradition, should guide how people live and are ruled. They met in coffee houses and salons, and their books spread by the printing press.

John Locke (1689) wrote that everyone has natural rights to life, liberty and property, and a government must protect them. Montesquieu (1748) said power should be split three ways, so no one holds it all.

Britain's colonies in North America paid taxes but had no members in Parliament: 'no taxation without representation'. After protests such as the Boston Tea Party (1773), they declared independence on 4 July 1776: 'all men are created equal'.

Yet slavery went on in the USA for almost 90 years. In France, people were hungry and the king was short of money. On 14 July 1789 a crowd stormed the Bastille. Then the Rights of Man said all men are born free and equal.

Not everyone was included: Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791). The revolution turned to the Terror (1793-94), when thousands were put to death. Napoleon took power in 1799, and wars spread across Europe until 1815.

In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose up in 1791; Toussaint Louverture became a leader. In 1804 they founded Haiti, the first nation made by people who had freed themselves. Simon Bolivar later led independence wars in South America.
Try it in the world: write your village's own declaration of rights on a sign: three rights everyone has, and who makes the laws. Ask friends to vote on it. Next: slavery and abolition.

exercises.prompt: Which thinker wrote about natural rights to life, liberty and property?
exercises.hint: He wrote in England in 1689, the year of the Bill of Rights.
exercises.explain: John Locke: natural rights to life, liberty and property.

exercises.prompt: In which year did the American colonies declare independence?
exercises.hint: It is celebrated every year on 4 July.

exercises.prompt: The storming of the Bastille happened in 1789.
exercises.hint: Remember the year the French Revolution began.
exercises.explain: True: 14 July 1789, now France's national day.

exercises.prompt: What did 'no taxation without representation' mean?
choices: no taxes unless we have a say in Parliament
exercises.hint: Representation means having someone who speaks for you where laws are made.
exercises.explain: The colonists would not pay taxes set by a Parliament where they had no members.

exercises.prompt: Match each thinker to the idea.
exercises.hint: Powers, women, tolerance, rights: who wrote which?
exercises.explain: Montesquieu: separation of powers. Wollstonecraft: women's rights. Voltaire: tolerance. Locke: natural rights.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: Compare the years: the smaller, the earlier.

exercises.prompt: The Declaration of Independence was signed in 1776; slavery ended in the USA in 1865. How many years later was that?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: Why was Haiti's independence in 1804 so important?
choices: it was the first country in Europe
people who had been enslaved founded a nation
exercises.hint: Think of who fought for it, and what they had been before.
exercises.explain: People who had freed themselves from slavery founded Haiti, the first such nation.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: the American Revolution or the French Revolution?
items: taxes with no say in Parliament
exercises.hint: One began over taxes in colonies; the other in Paris, against a king's rule at home.
exercises.explain: American: the Declaration of Independence, the Boston Tea Party, taxes with no say. French: the Bastille, the Rights of Man, the Terror.

exercises.prompt: Olympe de Gouges wrote that women should have the same rights as men.
exercises.hint: Think of the declaration she wrote in 1791.
exercises.explain: True: her Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791) claimed equal rights for women.

exercises.prompt: Which problem did the declarations of 1776 and 1789 leave unsolved?
choices: they left out women and enslaved people
they had no ideas about rights
exercises.hint: Ask who 'all men' really included at the time.
exercises.explain: Women could not vote and slavery went on: the rights were promised to some, not all.

exercises.prompt: Why did Montesquieu want three separate powers?
choices: so no one person holds all the power
exercises.hint: Think what could happen if one person made, ran and judged the laws.
exercises.explain: Split powers check each other, so no one can rule without limits.

exercises.prompt: Napoleon took power in 1799 and was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815. For about how many years did he rule?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: Put the French Revolution's events in order.
exercises.hint: It began with the Bastille and ended with an emperor's defeat.
exercises.explain: 1789 the Bastille, August 1789 the Rights of Man, 1793-94 the Terror, 1799 Napoleon, 1815 Waterloo.

exercises.prompt: The Enlightenment's ideas still shape constitutions today.
exercises.hint: Think of separate powers and rights in the constitutions you met in grade 7.
exercises.explain: True: rights and the separation of powers are in many constitutions, such as the USA's of 1787.
